BEFORE leaving the question of the Alabama
claims it may not be amiss to put before the
working, men of England a view of it
which May tend to explain the action of
our upper, or governing classes, at the com-
mencement and through the continuance of
the American struggle, as well as a suggestion
'or two as to how these claims should be met, in a
'Way worthy the consideration of those who in
.both countries are interested in the con-

tinuanee of peace—especially of those who
'labour with their hands for the purpose of

r:seOuring the means of life.
Lot it be borne in mind that the great ques-
tion of the present century is the "labour
question." flow the multitude who have no
eommodity hut their labour, shall regulate its
price so that they may live decently and com-
fortably without pressing too heavily on that
which is called profit by those, who as owners
'of capital, carry on manufacturing and mer-
cantile operations. And concurrently with
this, how best to govern and control the workers
that their proceedings may not interfere
vexatiously with the action of their employers.

- Trades Unicins are found to be trouble-
some in England, and are naturally greatly
disliked by employers of labour. The grow-
ng of the day amongst the
working people which is extending the spirit
of union, and making great trades organisations
possible---is also hated; and if the course of
events could be turned back, and old slavery
or serfdom in forni or in spiritrestored, nothing
Would, be more gratifying to those upper class
" respectable " people, whether in trade or out
Of it, who prize above all things the privilege
and power of being able to do "what they like
with their own."

Whoa the struggle began in America these
mefl instinctively understood its meaning.
They knew it was not in its essence a struggle
between North and South, or black and white.
The worker iu the position of a slave was the
removal of the man from his hu man status.
The conversion ' of the human creature into
capital, and by this means an end for ever to
the perplexing struggle between labour and
capital. The next step freely talked of was
the reduction of poor dependent whites to a
state approaching slavery, which, when
supplemented by Coolie importation, extending
Perhaps to Europe, the tide-stream of so-called
economic science stimulated by commercial
greed and class pride, would in time sweep
Way all resistance on the part of those
struggling for that form of civilisation which is
based on free labour and sustained by the
universal diffusion of education and liberty.
'those who were readers of our newspapers
during the American struggle must have seen
not once, but hundredsof times, stated by

our pro-Southern journals, dspecially the
Standard, Times, and Saturday Review, that
the cause of the slave-holders was the cause
of the aristocratic as against the democratic
principle. That the failure of the aristocratic
principle in America would lead to its ulti-
mate destruction in England, and that
therefore it was the duty of our upper class
"friends of order" to give such aid and
encouragement as they could to the political
and social principles upheld by the South.
It was in this spirit and for this object that
the disgraceful action which has led to our
present difficulties with America was set on
foot. It was through discreditable prejudices
such as these, that Alabamas, Sumters, and
Ploridas were sent on their dastardly errands
of destruction. And it was because of this
absolutely un-English hatred of popular right
and social liberty that the wretched Cotton
Loan was subscribed for.

The American people and the American
Government know this. But they must know
also that whilst we had amongst our ignorant
shopleeping classes, and our. passionately pre-
judiced upper and governing classes, this de-
testable and most mischievous spirit, we had
amongst the masses of our people at the same
time tho very opposite of this. A spirit of
loyalty to liberty and right, an earnest and
aetiire sympathy with them which never
failed, a desire for' their triumph, for the
integrity of their law, and the safety of their
country, which never suffered diminution
from the first to the last moment of their
most momentous struggle. At this time the

working men felt that the folly and mad-
ness of the upper classes would have some day
to be paid for. They had faith that the old
fight of light against darkness—of liberty
against slavery, in fact, of GOD against the
Devil, must end in triumph, and through this
belief they saw that the actual damage done
would have to be compensated. That America
could in justice claim compensation, simply
because she had wrongfully suffered loss, and
had a right to it. On this matter there is no
difference of opinion between the masses of
the English people, and the
.people of
America. And if any difference should arise
it will not be because we wish to escape the
.payment of a just debt, but solely and entirely
because unreasonable demands may be made
upon us. Nothing can have a worse effect
than an extravagance of this kind, as it will
turn the undoubted sympathy of the working
people of England now existing in favour of
America, into distrust, which, should a 'war
ensue, will be infallibly converted into hatre4 ;
and in the dark catalogue of national evils it
would be difficult to find a worse calamity
than this.

It- weak' be to the interest of both countries
to settle this matter, speedily, with as little,
huxtering and higgliug as possible, and to that
end nnolaims that are not perfectly valid in
their character ought
,to be put forward, nor
should any claim be resisted by England the
character of which is sustainable by legitimate
and sufficient evidence. But, presuming the
whole difficulty of examination and adj ustrnant
got through, then, and not till thou, will come
Up a question in the discussion of which the
working men of England will have to take an
important part; narnoly, the question as to
how the money is to be raised for the purpo.so
of paying this debt to America.

Tinu iniquitous wars which England has
waged against China have been commercial
wars. Wars deliberately undertaken by the
British Government to open out fresh markets
for the sale of the products of our manufactur-
ing industries, and by means whereof some-
thing might be done to stave off the political
difficulties, which seemed to be growing more
and more urgent. There was not a shadow of

justification or excuse for these wars. They
have covered the English name with infamy.
This infamy continues, because the wrongs,
for which we fought those wicked wars,
remain. We still infliot these wrongs by force
upon the Chinese people, and our present
Government has publicly in Parliament and
in the name of the English people, justified the
o mtinnance of these wrongs. I shall there-
fore go at length into the subject. I want to
awaken a consciousness of our guilt in the
, breasts of English workmen.
' Our conduct towards the Chinese has not
been that of one civilised nation to another. It
was thought-that as the Chinese civilisation
was inferior to the English, there was' no
necessity for our conduct being regulated by
the ordinary principles of just dealing, The
opening of Chinese markets for English goods,
was an end which, to commercial eyes,
appeared su.fueient to justify any moans. It
was looked upon as the right of an English-
man to buy and sell wherever he chose. And
if an ignorant and uncivilised people did not
want English goods, they must be taught by
force the advantages which they could not
otherwise see. They were not to be free to
decline the benefits of intercourse and trade
with England. It was to be and is now, free
trade imposed by English fern. But we
ought to remember the vigorous opposition
which Datum audj COBDEN offered to the last
Chinese war. Unfortunately in the Session
of 1870, when Ur. GLlDs.roxE and Mr,.
GRANT purl defended our uonauot with

respect to the Chinese, Mr. BRIGHT was away..
I trust that his voice will be once more heara
upon this subject in thf.gouse of Cennmons.
China is a world in itolf An elaborate in-
dustrial system has grown, up during a long
course of ages. In that 704 Empire there is
a complete interchange Of the products and
the eonarnodities of its different districts and
its varied climate, fully adequate to supply all
the wants of the Chinese people, and render-
ing trade with foreign nations quite unneces-
sary for. material comfort, or for pcogress.
Their real Want is that of seientifie knowledge.
The Chinese Government were well aware how
great a temptation trade with China was to
England. -They know what the conduct of
England had been to other Eistern nations.
They, knew that El.iglall4 had begun by simple
trading with India, and then had seized upon

ann&xing novv provinces. They were fully

*the West with the East; they feared the re-

and therefore the Chinese government believed
that while England had -a groat deal to gain
front commercial intercourse, any such pro-
eeeding. would .be fraught with grave and
Serious danger to China. Their worst fears
have been fully realised.' Our conduct has
been violent and rapacious, whereas the
Chinese Government, in thy opinion, has, from
first to last, [toted with wisdom and modera-
tion, all the more praiseworthy because they
Combined admirable firmness With mild and
gentle forbearance.

The object of the development of our indus-
trial system and the employment of our poor,
by opening out fresh markets for English
manufactures, is,: in itself, a dasirablo and
proper object for statesmen to aim at. But it
must be done peaceably, with a duo regard to
justice, in a spirit of fair dealing and voluntary
agreement. If we had preserved towards these
Eastern nations an attitude of equality, or of
honest
.dealing,
,all would have been well.
We have,' howevt r, pursued n totally different
plan. We have not merely adopted a tone
.auperiority and overbearing ascendancy,
but we have set aside all the ordinary rules of
moral conduct. ,We have treated the Chinese
with cruel injustice. We have played the part
of bullies and robbers. These aro very strong
expressions, but the facts .are stronger. I
invite the attention of working men to these facts,
Which I shall endeavour in the several articles
I Shall write, testate as clearly as loan. The
story of these proceedinga is somewhat intri-
cate and ditlioult to tell shortly. • But if the
facts are involved, the political question is not.
Statesmen make it very difficult, because
they refuse to deal with it on moral grounds
From the moral stand-point it is only too clear.
Up to the year 1833, the trade with China
was in the bands of the East India Company.
After that time the privilege of the Company
came to an end, and the trade was thrown
open. The trade had passed .entirely by way
of Canton, and was regulated by an English
superintendent on the one hand, and by
certain merchants, called the Hong merchants,
on behalf of the Chinese traders. The English
Government desired that the regulation of the
trade should be in the hands of a Government
official, and accordingly they appointed Lord
NarrEa to superintend the trade, and he
insisted upon holding intercourse and treating
with the local- authorities Instead of the
Hong merchants. But this was in direot
violation of the Chinese law. The CLinese
Government had come to the wise determina-
tion, that they would not have these arrange-
ments political, but solely commercial. Lord
NAprita, placing himself in antagonism to
these views, refused to receive the Hong
Merchants, who were in fact the authorised
officials on behalf of the Chinese.'Empire. In
coniequenee of which, the Hong merchants,
acting ureter the advice and direction of the
Imperial authoritieS, stopped the trade alto-
gether. ‘. Lord NAP= then took the extra-
ordinary step of placarding the walls of
Canton with a proclamation of such singular
insolenee towards the Chinese antherites as
alone would have justified his immediate and.
for3ible expulsion."
This, then, was the bcgittnintof our extra- -
torttinfuly trnel ,nutragef,44 policy - toward,

China. Lord NAPIEft was the.first to adopt,
as the national policy of England, that which
had before been only the wieh and object of
private Merchants. lie deliberately proposed
to the English Government a scheme of vio-
lent aggression, which he proceeded to carry
into effect. The following extracts from his
own letters to,. the Government show the
spirit in which he conducted himself shortly
before he took, ose war-like proceedings of
1834, which constituted a grave and serious
aggression by England upon China. Lord
NAPIER writes :

"Four ediots have been let, or against me
for landing without a 'red chop or permit.
I have been order zd off, and entreated to de-
part ; yet with all this they have not yet
taken me and sent me down the river. Sup-
pose a Chinaman, or any other man, were to
land under similar circumstances at White-
'hall, your Lordship would not allow him to
loiter, as they have permitted me. Looking
at the utter imbecility of this Government, I
.cannot for one . moment suppose that in
treating with such a nation Her MAJESTY'S Go-
vernment will be ruled by the ordinary forms
prescribed among civilised people." "Her
MAJESTY'S Government should consult imme-
meciiately on the best plan for conmanding a
commercial treaty." "Demand the Same per-
-send privileges for all traders that every
trader enjoys in England. This, no doubt,
would be a very staggering proposition in the
face of a red chop;' but say to the EMPEROR,
adopt this, or abide the consequences, and it
is done. Now, abiding the consequences
immediately presupposes. all the horrors of a
bloody war against a defenceless people."
"Such an undertaking would be worthy the
greatheas. and the power of England."
Now I ask working men to ponder over
this. Then they will appreciate why it is
necessary to reiterate again and again the
truism that politics must be subordinated to
morals, that our political acts must be regu-
lated by moral considerations, and that this is
the revolution which is so urgently needed
before a new international policy can be
constructed.

There are some persons who think it useless
to examine these wrongs, which they. say are of
the past. But I say that they are not, that they
are not old scars or healed wounds; they are
continuing sores, which corrode and eat into
our national life. We must lay them bare,
and probe them to the source and seat of
disease, painful and shameful though the
process may be. The men who have been
guilty of these things have been rewarded.
We reap an enormous money profit from our
iniquity. They are the wages of sin, though
they are vindicated by Mr. GLADSTONE and
his Government, and the Houses of Parlia-
ment.

HENRY CROMPTON.

QUESTIONS BY A POSITIVIST.

As a kind of comment upon my recent
papers in the BEE-lIIVE, I have received a series
of questions, in which an opportunity is given
to compare the views which I advocate with
those of a rival school of social reformers, but
which I hope will be won over to my views,
when I can succeed in making them under-
stood. For in many respects our general
objects are the same. The writer of theSe
questions is a learned friend, who has.long been
a very zealous Positivist, but who, as his
. questions show, has not yet attended stiff.;
eiently to what may be called the Causational
system to be able .to see, and through seeing
to feel, its ineomparable superiority over all,
other views of social reform. (It may be called
the Causational system, to distinguish it from
other forms of socialism, because it differs'
fundamentally from many parts of the views
which are commonly designated as socialism,
and because it is the practical application of
the knowledge of the causes of evil and of
good to man. And it cannot be called Owen-
ism, because, •although it includes all that is
true in the views of OWE, and Nfas founded
by him, it excludes the errors by which his
ideas were to a great extent and very mis-
chievously falsified.) And, as in these ques-
tions leading- points are referred to in which
Positivists suppose that their system is greatly
superior to Causationisna, but. iu which in fact,
the latter is infinitely before the Other, it will

be very useful to reply to them in the BEE-
HIVE, in which I have lately been strongly
recommending the latter. And I do moste'coa-
dently recommend it,upon grounds offact, which
cannot be questioned when they are under-
stood, as the only means by which the working
classes, and all classes, can be delivered from
the evils of a system which is false in its

foundation, and in every part of its super-
structure except so far as in the nature of

things it can only modify injuriously, and
cannot entirely exclude, what is right.
First Question.—Js not the present state of
society the result of the slow progression of
the past, by the inevitable law of progress;
and can it therefore be expected that any
single reformer can at once make a funda-
mental change in society by means of books,
lectures, or a society? Was present society
formed thus?

Answer.—The slow progress Of society in the
past has been in accordance with the law of
progress during the period in which the causes
of evil have been in operation to counteract
the instinctive struggles of man for the attain-
ment of good, intellectually, morally, and
materially. His moral as well as his material
progress has been dependent upon intellectual
advancement. And hitherto his advancement
has been chiefly.. material, because it has been
chiefly in the material sciences and arts that
he has advanced intellectually. But even in
material, progress he has not yet advanced so
far as to be able to prevent very wide-spread
poverty and fear of poverty, and all their
miserable consequences, although ho has
obtained in great superabundance all the
material moans to effect this result. And
why is he still thus physically helpless?
Because he is still ignorant and in error in
reference to the causes of evil and of good in
the production and distribution of wealth—
this ignorance and error being the primary
cause of evil in this department of the business
of life—and because he is also in ignorance
and error in reference to the causes of evil and
of good in the formation of character, and he
cannot therefore have the intellectual. and
moral character which is necessary for the
beneficial regulation of economics and of
human affairs in general.
And his effectual moral advancement has
been prevented by the absence of the intellec-
tual progress upon which it is dependent, Ho
could not make any great improvement in his
moral condition while he remained in. ignor-
anoe and error in reference to the causes of
evil and of good in the formation of character.
For this ignorance and error constitute the '
, primary cause of evil in the development and
direction of his moral nature. Hence it has
been that moral education has always been to
a great extent a failure, and that the more
educated are in general no better morally
than those who are called uneducated, and
are very often much worse. And hence
it is that the worst feelings of badly
educated human nature—selfishness, deception
(or dishonesty), malevolence, ignorant irasci-
bility, vindictiveness—aro so often found, in
various combinations, under an exterior which
is highly "civilised.". And that in actual
moral goodness the most civilised nations, so
called, are in many respects little in advance
of those whom they call savage or uncivilised,
and are often, in some respects, much behind
them. And that even the kindest and most con-
scientious are always, to some extent, morally
disfigured by the injurious feelings and the
erroneous ideas which are the necessary effects
or education in ignorance and error in refer-
ence to the causes of evil and of good. And
while this primary cause of moral evil remains
in operation, progress Must inevitably be as
slow as it has hitherto been.

It is obvious that an immense:change will
be made in the state of things when the
knowledge of the causes of evil and of good,
which will be the primary cause of good, is
introduced, and when, by its introduction, the
ignorance of these causes, and the erroneous
ideas respecting them, the primary cause of
evil, are removed. This will be an intellectual
revolution, an intellectual new birth, in man.
And in due tune it will produce a moral new
birth. The preparation for it has been
6; slow ;" but when the time for its aeeorn-
pliehtnent is come, the event will be like the

coming of the minor changes by which it has
been preceded—as, for instance, the cornmencsment and development of the railway
system. It could not take place while the
causes of evil and of good were unknown.
It cannot but take place (not "at once," but
progressively) when these causes are known,
in those of the present generation who have not
been too much deteriorated intellectually and
morally. And the highly improved intellectual
and moral character which men and women
will thus acquire will cause them to make
coixesponding changes in 'their institutions,
arrangements, and general proceedings.
A "single reformer," ROBERT OWF4rs wee
the discoverer, though imperfectly, of the new
knowledge. It remained too imperfect for
general practical application for more than
fifty years. It 18 now perfected sufficiently'
for general practical application, when it can
be sufficiently disseminated "by mono °f
books, lectures, a society, &c."
"Present society" was not " forma thus j"
just as the development of the old roads Nvus
very different from the construction
of the
railways. And it is obvious that we can"
not judge of the progress which will take
place when the causes of good are ptetolit'
from that which has taken place in their
absence, and while the causes of evil were
dominant over man's destiny. There will
still, as stated in my table or list of condi.
tions, be "endless improvement and Iv'
gress ;" but it will be under the law of pro-
gress with the presence of the chief causes af
good, as one of the conditions, instead of being
under the domination of the Causes of evil, ia
man himself and in his surroundings.

THE PARKS.

VERNON HARCOURT has done good
.666'6 in exposing to public indignation Mr.
ArRTON'S Park Bill, the real object of which
18 to give the authorities power to stop

were held for the purpose of protesting
ugainst any proposed act of the Government.
Mr. HARCOURT is quite right in stating in the i
Rouse of. Commons that the Parks Bill s a
'direct infringement of Magna Charta. By
this Charter of our liberties, the ruling powers
are bound down to maintain and preserve the
liberty of the press, the liberty of speech,
and the liberty of the person—that is to '
say, that none of these rights shall be
interfered with, except through the verdict of
jgrY.: By the proposed act of Mr.
AYRTOII, a set of Park keepers, not the
regular police, but men appointed by the
Ranger, the Duke of Cambridge, and com-
posed in a great part of butlers, coachmen,
and other servants of the aristocracy, are to
have the power of causing the incarceration of
any man in the Park whom they may consider
acting improperly, and with whose name and
residence they are unacquainted. Such is one
of the clauses of Mr. AYRTON'S Bill, the great
Object of which throughout is to stop from the
eonamencement any assemblage which may
grow into a public meeting. I fully admit
that the Parks must be kept freo from black-
guardisra of every species; but why not leave
this to
...the regular police, who now do
4114' inSal the Parks? Ig it right that dea. I

r paid power should be given to a set of men—
not even regular policemen—nominated by the
DUKE of CAMBRIDCFE, and entirely under orders
and regulations, framed by Mr. AYRTOI7, and
enforced by the Royal DUKE as Ranger, for
which sinecure he receives from the people a
salary and the profit derived from the grass
let out to butchers, and that in addition to his
large allowance as a member of the Royal
Family,

I maintain that it is the right of the people
of London to assemble in public meeting when
they please, in order to state their grievances
to Parliament, and it is the duty of the
Government to provide a fitting place for such
assemblages. There is no better place for this than
Primrose Hill. If Government would declare
that all peaceful and well-conducted meetings
assembled on Primrose Hill would not be inter-
fered with by the police, then they might
without impropriety declare that no meeting
of any kind should be held in Hyde Park or
any of the Parks of London. The last public
meeting which was held on Primrose Hill, was
during the time GARIBALDI was in London.
The meeting was held for the purpose of pro-
testing against the conduct of the Government
in compelling GARIBALDI to leave England in
' compliance with the wishes of the late Emrrnon
of the French. Upon this occasion the Govern-
ment, at the head of which was Lord PALMERSTON,
ordered the meeting to be dispersed by the
police, which was effected in the most brutal
manner. Since then no meeting has been
attempted at Primrose Hill. But I repeat, if
Government would declare that no properly-
conducted meeting would be interfered with
on Primrose Hill, then I am fully of opinion
that the people of London would be perfectly
satisfied, and would not insist to hold meet-
ings in Hyde Park.

EPPING FOREST.

Ori Tuesday evening a public meeting was
held in St. James's-hall, Piccadilly, in aid of
the steps which are being taken for the pre-
servation of Epping Forest for the inhabitants
of the metropolis, and with special reference
to the Epping Forest Bill and the Metage of
Grain (Port of London) Bill, now standing for
second reading in the House of Commons, the
object of which is to secure a surrender of the;
manorial and other privato rights in conside-
ration of a commutation duty on grain of one
farthing per cwt. The Bills being introduced
by the Corporation of London, the powerful
municipal influence of the City will he ex-
erted in Parliament on the side of the public.
The chair was taken by Lord G. Hamilton,

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings,
said they were met to endeavour to save what
remained of Epping Forest from the hands of
the spoiler, and express their approval of the.
manner in which the Corporation of London
had taken up the question. (Cheers.) He
Was glad to see so many inhabitants of West-
minster trying to help their brethren at the
East-end, and ho regarded such a gathering
as a protest against all attempts to deprive the
people of the metropolis and its vicinity of
open spaces. (Cheers.)
On the motion of Mr. Frederick Young,
seconded by Mr. A. Johnson, M.P., the fol-
lowing resolution was adopted unanimously—
That this meeting, recognising the paramount
necessity of Open Spaces being kept in all large
cities as a means of promoting and preserving the
health, as well as the enjoyment of the great
masses of the people, desires to record its opinion
that it is essential to preserve Epping Forest as
an open space for ever for the health and recrea-
tion of the inhabitants of London."

The Rev. Mr. Hastings, of Wanstead,
moved the following—
That this meeting expresses its thanla to the
Corporation of the City of London for the active
and energetic steps it has already taken to main-
tain the rights of the people and to save the
Forest from destruction ; and also pledges itself to
support the Forest Fund' established to use all
constitutional means for the accomplishment of
this noble and necessary object."

The resolution was seconded by 'Arr. James
Beal, and agreed to ; after which a petition to
Parliament in accordance with the objects of
the meeting was adopted, and the proceedings
terminated with a vote of thanks to the noble
lord in the chair.

The nineteenth anniversary of the London

-
Association of Foremen Engineers and Draughts-
_

moil was celebrated by a public dinner at the
City Terminus Hotel, on Saturday, the 17th
instant. It was remarkably successful in all ways,
but the intermixture of distinguished visitors
with the ordinary members of the institution, and
the genuine good feeling apparent on all hands,
constituted the most gratifying features of the
evening's proceedings. James Howard, Esq.,
M.P., presided, and he was assisted by Sir Spencer
Robinson, Lord Eloho, M.P.; Captain Beaumont,
31. P. ; B. Samuelson, M.P. ;Professor Tyndall, C.B. ;
Vignoles, Esq., F.R.S., vice-president of the In-
stitution of Civil Engineers; John R. Ravenhill,
Esq., C.E. ; IL J. Slack, Esq.; Mr. Joseph
Newton, C.E., president of the Association, and
many other well known gentlemen.

The speeches generally were above the average
of those usually delivered after dinner, and Mr.
Newton urged employers of engineering labour
to attend the meetings of their foremen, and share
in the discussions thereat more frequently.
Professor Tyndall's address was admirably
adapted to the occasion, and the chairman per-
formed his task with considerable ability.
The musical arrangements of the evening, con-
ducted by Mr. F. A. Bridge, were very satisfac-
tory, and a song, written we believe, by the
president of the Association, entitled "Our
Foremen Engineers," was enthusiastically re-
ceived. The last verse of this effusion runs as
follows :

"Should wrongful claims affront our land,
And Cousins choose to fight,
Our Woolwich guns and iron-clads
Will show Great Britain's might.
With Whitworth, Field, and Ravenhill,
With Armstrong, Penn, and Reed,
Old England's groat men to the fore,
What more can Foremen need!"

It was near to Sunday morning when the
audience, numbering about 300, retired from the
Groat Hall of the Hotel.

The humble Petition of the Trades' Council of

Leeds, in the County of York,

Showeth,—That your petitioners, having taken
Into consideration the result of legislation on
trades societies during the last session of Parlia-
ment, are firmly of opinion that it has signally
failed in effecting the objects previously antici-
pated; that the exceptional and vague character
of the penal clauses of the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act establishes a new catalogue of law-
created crimes, which are aimed at workmen in
combination, but when committed by other

criminal.

That with this view we are strongly convinced

insidiously aims a blow at the liberties of trade
organisations whilst it has a tendency to foster
and strengthen a feeling of antagonism towards
workmen on the part of employers.

disapproval of the aforesaid Act, and earnestly
call upon your Honourable House to at once
repeal the causes relating to coercion and molesta-
tion, and thus place the members of trade societies
on an equality before the law in common with the
rest of the community; and at the same time we
express our fixed determination not to rest satisfied
until this has been accomplished.

And your petitioners, as in duty bound, wil
ever pray, &c., &o.

LANCASHIRE.

RAILWAY GOODS CLERKS AND THEIR WAGES.

On Saturday evening, a meeting of representa-
tives of clerks employed at the several stations on
the East Lancashire section of the Lancashire and
Yorkshire Company's lino was held at the Eagle
and Child Hotel, Blackburn. The various speakers
who addressed the meeting asserted that the goods
clerks were worked sadly too long, and that they
were very badly remunerated. After considerable
discussion, the meeting unanimously resolved,
"That a petition be forwarded to the board of
directors of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Rail-
way Company asking for an advance of 20 per
cent. all round, and that a committee be appointed
to carry the matter to a successful issue." It was
also decided that the advance should be asked to
be given immediately, and that the committee
should decide what steps should be taken by the
clerks in the event of the directors refusing to
comply with the request.

ROSSENDALE.
STRIKE OP WOOLLEN BLOCK PRINTERS.

On Friday last the printers in the employ of
Messrs. Taylor and Ormerod, the extensive felt
carpet printers, at the Bridge End Mill, Now-
church, came out on strike for more wages. The
printers have each.a lad when working, whose duty
it is to supply the " succour" with dye, but
owing to the new Factory Act which has recently
come in force, these lads have to attend school half
day, and there being a scarcity of lads, the printers
have to pay more out of their pockets in order to
secure an additional half-timer. Messrs. Taylor
and Ormerod have offered the mon 10 per cent.
more, which they refuse to take. A few months
ago, the men were allowed 5 per cent more wages.
The printers in the employ of this firm earn on an
average £3 per week.

VALLEY OF THE DON.

DISPUTE IN TUE POTTERY TRADE.

An entirely new phase has occurred in the dis-
pute between the "fiat pressers" employed in the
pottery manufactories at Rotherham, Swinton,
Mexbro' and the Valley of the Don, and their
masters. It appears that the "flat pressers" em-
ployed at the Holmes Pottery, Rotherham, have
given their masters a month's notice to leave, in
consequence of, they allege, their being told that
the proprietors of that pottery would not concede
any of the points asked by the men, even though
the other masters in the district gave way, The
employes at another establishment have also given
in their notices, as they state that their masters
have made imputations that they have been guilty
of unscrupulous conduct in their work, in order
to deceive them. A meeting, at which the whole
of the pottery manufacturers of the district were
represented, Was held at Rotherham on Friday,
when it was contended that the men of two firms
only giving notice to leave was an act of injustice.
After some conversation it was resolved that
unless the men employed at the Holmes Pottery
withdraw their notices, or the whole of the work-
men at the other establishments give notice, the
masters will take the initiative and give the whole
of the flat pressers in the district a month's warn-
ing to leave their employment. The revised list
of prices which the men sent for consideration
by the masters was not taken notice of.

A crowded meeting of bricklayers and carpenters
engaged in and about the town of Maidstone took

evening last. Mr. Tomliu was unanimously voted

(excepting the first mile, which should be walked
in the man's own time) ; that overtime be paid for
during the first two hours at thin) and a quarter,
and after that at time and a half; that work done

. "Equality before the law" is the right of trades
and of men, and where the law or the admiuistra-
tion of the law, or the partial exercise of power,
presses unduly upon an individual or a trade, the
injustice is patent, and remedial measures become
imperatively necessary.
The mat and matting trade is and has long been
suffering under this infliction of wrong to an
extent beyond all other trades, resulting in a
decrease of 30 per cent. in wages, and threatening
its members with pauperisation or starvation.
The Legislature and the Magistracy, in their
desire to effect a reduction of the rates for support-
ing the criminal population of our gaols, have
deemed it right to vary the sentences to hard
labour passed upon criminals by substituting
industrial employment of a remunerative character.
The manufacture of mats and matting gives
partial employment to about 3,000 honest work-
men, ftt wages scarcely enabling them to support
themselves and their families.
The demand for their labour has been materially
and prejudicially affected by the competition of
the convicted criminals, who have been for some
years instructed in our gaols, to the extent of over
2,000 annually; and the remuneration of honest
labourers in the free labour market has been re-
duced by the rates of the gaol-manufactured
articles, at a price below:even the cost of the raw
material.
There is, consequently, no demand in the free
labour market for the hands discharged from our
gals ; whilst this wilful and cruel interference
With the natural and legitimate employment of
honest artisans cannot but result in the destruc-
tion of their trade, and of the spirit of honest in-
dependence of the innocent victims of so absurd a
system.
The advantage of a reduction of the gaol rate
at the cost of a proportionate increase in the poor's
rate is more than questionable.
The.isserifloe of 3,000 honest .operatives, that
2,000 rogues may annually be taught a trade
Which they cannot live by after their liberation, is
a ,wanton injustice.
It is true that the mat trade is, relatively to

Other trades, comparatively insignificant. Those
, 'who -depend upon it for a livelihood are few in
number, and of scant means for defence against
Official Wrong. But with honourable men these
circumstances would be a 'wall of defence and a
claialt,to protection. It was so in the recent case of
th!inateh-boz makers, and the power of the Im-
devernment quailed before the popular
80138 a of common humanity. Shall it be said that
none but the strong have a claim to fair play and
isst'treatnient P It would not be so held in a
connfry where Christianity is unknown, much less
can it be maintained under the constitutional
lunnarohy of our Christian Queen.
If the desirableness of the employment of our
conviets in remunerative labour be admitted in
order to the reduction of the gaol rate, the labour
whisk is most remunerative, all other things being
6(1101, should be: preferred, which would not be
roSt-making. The Directors Of Convict Prisons
report, on the authority of the Governor of Mill-
bank prison (p; 33), that in 18G0 the average daily
earnings of the mat-makers were sevenpenee ;
basket-nrkers, sevenpenco three-farthings ; shoe -
niakers*ciie shilling and a penny farthing; brush-
makers, ono shilling and threepence three.
farthings; (=Pars, one abilling and fourpence ;
tailors, one,Shilling and sevenpence farthing; and
tin.arnithi, three shillings and three-halfpence.
It is Clear, therefore, that from this standpoint the
eMployment of the convicts in raat.making .is not
in the interest of the ratepayers.

llor can it be seriously contended that it is', in
the interest of the convicts themselves. On their
discharge they can only, at the best, have acquired
an imperfect knowledge of a craft inferior in
Monetary importance to most, if not all others;
Rnat With this disadvantage, they will have to
swell the number of unemployed artisans who are
masters of their tradeoin. t'4 willing to work, though
ilaable to ()Wain employment.

What justification can the Government, or what
excuse can the Magistracy of Yorkshire advance
for their persistent persecution of the insignificant
trade of mat-makers? Utterly crushed out of
the free market of honest industry it may easily
be, if the indefensible acts of the executive be
sustained by the Legislature.

The compulsory manufacture of a surplus supply
of any marketable commodity is a violation of
every principle of political economy. The sys-
tematic adoption of the oppressive practice under
review is equivalent to a declaration by Govern-
ment to flood the mat-making market with a sur-
plus of labour utterly destructive of a defenceless
and unoffending class, asking only for leave to
work that they may live.

And the Governmental manufacturers of mats
and matting enter the field of competition against
honest labour with an absolute monopoly. They
have to meet no charge for labour—no item of
wages. Suppose a free-labour mat to cost a shil-
ling in raw material, and a shilling in wages to
the artisan, his employer cannot well retail it for
less than two shillings and a penny; whilst the

gaoler can afford to sell a precisely similar mat,
costing Lim a shilling, for thirteen pence, or any
sum between that and double the amount! No

trade can long exist, struggle as it may, under
such conditions. Nor can any Legislature, abet-
ting or sanctioning so iniquitous a system, enjoy
or deserve the continued respect of a justice-loving

community.
Under all the circumstances of the case,
it naturally follows that the trade consider
themselves the victims of official persecution.
They think that if the principle of competitive
manufacture is to be maintained as between con-
vict labour and the free labour of honest artisans,
one particular trade should not have been specially
subjected to that disadvantage, but that then
should be some degree of approximation to a
relative proportion among the several industrial
sections of the community. As contrasted with
the shoemakers or the tailors, the Mat-makers of
the metropolis are but as one to forty—a disparity
which would be vastly increased if the arca of
comparison were extended over the kingdom. If
then, 810 convicts, say in Wakefield Prison, had
to be put to renumerative labour, equitably
divided between those three trades, 10 should be

Mat-makers, 400 Shoemakers, and 400 Tailors ;
whercal, on the equitable apportionment of the
Wakefield justices in 1359, we find only 37 shoe-
makers and 36 tailors to 810 Mat-maker, instead
of 11 Mat. makers, 442 shoemakers, and 411
tailors! This is veritable persecution ! And as' if
to outrage propriety yet further, arid to outrage
every feelingof common sense. and common jusitce,
the ratepayers of Yorkshire have been taxed
thousands of pounds for the purchase, erection,
and working of steam-engines and power-looms
for the manufacture of Mats and Matting, and the
more speedy and effsetual ruin of tbo legitimate
trade and•pauperisation of all connected with it;
whilst to force a sufficient sale of the produce of
this unrighteous Monopoly, the gaol managers

employ travellers 1,) scour tho country for custo-
mers at prices below the cost, with a system of
discount upon purchases fir in excess of any ever
previously heard of in the trade.

THE PARKS' REGTILLTION BILL.

On Saturday evening, a numerously-attended
representative meeting, convened by the Committee
of the Public Rights Defence Association, an
organisation comprising gentlemen of all orders of
political opinions, was held at the Sussex Hall,
Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, for the purpose of
considering the best means of staying the future
progress of the Parka' Regulation Bill in the
House of Commons. Mr. Hartwell was called to
the chair, and amongst those present were a num-
ber of gentlemen who have taken an active and
leading part in the Reform agitation of 1866-7,
and upwards of 40 delegates from as many
politic al, social, and non-political organizations.
The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, ex-
plained the reason inducing the committee to cull
the meeting, and stated letters had been received
from a number of gentlemen, members of Parlia-
ment and others, regretting their inability to
attend the meeting, but promising them hearty
co-operation. They were met not for speech-
making, but for business. They were met to
defeat a Bill which he believed all present deemed
one of the most unconstitutional that had been
presented to Parliament since the days of Sidrnouth
and Castlereagh. (Hear.) This was not a party
question, the ultra-Conservative and the Red
Republicans being equally interested in upholding
the fight of public meeting, the freedom of
speech, and the liberty of the people. (Hear.) If
this Bill passed into law as it at present stood,
all these rights would be at the mercy of
one man irresponsible to Parliament for his
actions. The Bill made almost every conceivable
act performed in the parks, however harmless in
itself, if done contrary to the "rules of the park,',
a penal offence, subjecting the person so offending
to be arrested by a park-keeper without warrant

and to fine and imprisonment. (Shame.) The
Bth clause in the Bill was specially directed
against holding a meeting or delivering an address
not only in Hyde-park, but in all the other metro-
politan and suburban parks or greens, including
even Primrose-hill. (Hear.) The person in
whom was vested the power of making the "rules
of the park," was either the Ranger, or, where no
such officer existed, the Commissioner of Public
Works. He did not think anyone present would
like to be subjected to any rules likely to be
framed by the present holder of the office of
Commissioner of Public Works. (Hear.)
Captain Maxse strongly denounced the Bill.
All persons, however extreme • their opinions, had
a right to express their views at a legally con-
, veiled public meeting. As
.these persons, were
denied the use of the public halls, and the. Bill
proposed to deny them the right of meeting in the.
parks, they were virtually prevented from holding
a public meeting at all. (Hear.)
Dr. Langley said that portion of Hyde-park
where public meetings had been held was heftily
ever used by the visitors to the patk, and would
inconvenience no one. No cases of disturbance
had ever occurred at those political meetings in
the parks, save in the instance where the disttirli:
ance was brought eh...nit by the action of the
police at the time the railings fell down. (Um.)
Mr. G. Odger said the people had obtained the
recognition of the right of meeting in Hyde Park
while the Tories were in office, and they were not
going to allow a sham Liberal Government to
take it away from them. Some of the Ablest men

of the Tory party, such as Mr. Henley,* the
member for Oxfordshire, denounced the bill
Algerine Act. He could say nothing stronger.
(Hoar).

Tho proceedings then took the form of a discus-
sion, in which ihe leading preceding speakers, and
also Messrs. Horton, Stainsby, Facey, Hennessy,
Shipton, Fairbairn, Cromer, Tolemash, Lyons,
Pottle, Taplin, Hughes, Mottershead, and others
took part, and ultimately the following resolutions
were unanimously adopted

I. " That this meeting of representatiVo men of
various classes and political opinions, convened

,
-
for tho purpose of considering the Parks Regula-
Bill, introduced into Parliament by Mr. Ayr ton,
the Commissioner of Works, as a member of the

Government, is of opinion that many of the pro-
visions of such bill are frivolous and Vexatious,
while others are of the most arbitrary and uncan-
stitutional character, suppressing the riglit of public
meeting and freedom of speech, and curtailing the
liberties of the people; and is further of opinion,
that the introduction Of the said bill is a disgrace
to the Government, and a gross insult to, and
wanton defiance of, the people. That such a
measure, if passed into law, would create a danger-
ous centralisation of power in the Government,
tending to subvert the principal of municipal
freedom. That, therefore, this meeting pledges
itself to take immediate and energetic actions to
atop the further progress of this obnoxious bill,

and earnestly invite the co•operation of all parties
and classes in the movement."

2. "That this meeting tenders it hearty thanks
to Mr. Vernon Harcourt, M.P. for Oxford, for his
manly and vigorous opposition to the above bill in
his place in Parliament, and his well deserved
strictures upon the conduct of the Government in
relation thereto; and also records its thanks to
those members who voted against the second read-
ing of the bill. That it calls upon the HOMO of
Commons, irrespective of party, to record their
votes against the bill in all its future stages, and
will consider all members voting in favour of, the
bill, or absenting themselves from divisions, al
utterly unworthy the confidence of the people in
the future."

3. "That the chairman be requested to write to
Mr. Gladstone, asking him to receive 'a
deputation
on an early day, to urge upon the Government the
unconditional withdrawal of the bill."

4. "That Messrs. Mottershead, Horton, Osborne,
Shipton, Pottle, Stainsby, Hartwell, Elliott, rimy,
and Evans, be a sub-committee, to wait upon
members of Parliament, asking them to make use
of all the forms of the House to defeat the bill."
The question of a great public demonstration in
Hyde Park was then considered, but it was agreed
that this subject should stand over until the
result of the application to Mr. Gladstone was
ascertained.

The meeting was then adjourned until Tuesday
evening.

WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
roil PROMOTING TIIE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE

TO THE WORKING CLASSES OP GREAT BRITAIN.

FELLOW :WOIMMEN,--

The Working Men's Committee has been formed
•in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the House of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. He was met with the objec-
tion that' tho OaSe of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendoWment and disestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Miall, that ho must first convince a majority
of tho people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
boon accepted; and the Society for the _Liberation
of Religion front State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro-
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, after thobroad challenge thrown
down by the Fromier,i they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain 'front
a declaration of their honest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
loader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Men, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon tho purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr.' Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the pis-
endowment and Disestablishmont of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, 'whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody 'a faithful and com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the 'challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These, then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.

The views of the Committee may be thus con.
sisely stated--

1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must bo left between man and his Maker.
2. They are of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been disestablished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
Kingdom _ ,
3, They era persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has Utterly
failed to accomplish the task for which it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects whieh churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Protestantism or the then
State-Church, 'the great majority of the I3ritish
People are either members of the different Pro-
t,estant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Churoh,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish-
ment.

5. The immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance ; because
those revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation, are distributed among the
religious teachers of half; or less than half, of the
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries

and emoluments are paid to 13ishops and other
Dignitaries, while, .of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the feu cat
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations. '
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additioaal reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that of
the, Establishment in Which they have so strong
vested interest. Hence, in ovary agitation of $
political or social character, they are always en
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of national
weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good men uniting, as
they otherwise might unite, in works of philan-
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life.

Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious canslderatie?l
of their fellow workmen throughout the counts/.
In order to ascertain and give effect to their vieYts,
Branch Committees will be formed, and meetings
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and believed'
that the practical result will be that, after this
great questionlas been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the House of Commons,
Mr. Midi will be in a position to give to Mr'
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Working
Men's Committee, Yours faithfully,
GEORGE HOWELL (ChairmAn)*
DANIEL GUILE (Treasurer).
Geonuu Porran (Secretary).

The motion on the appointment of Sin ROBERT

Upon a "colourable qualification," to de-

This was the case against Ministers which

Of from the fact, that, notwithstanding the
largeness of the majority supposed on other

was the game to spoil which Sir ROUNDELL

There is no getting rid, however, of the fact,

MR, 1141,0Przlas been the first in the present
session tel.tevive the question af emigration.
He referred principally to South Africa and
West Australia, IYeth together having an un
reclaimed acreage Opal to what the 'United
States have at their disposal.• Were these
lands divided in equal portions among the
- Scotch, and Irish subjects of her
'ding in all parts of the world,
101101, and child would liar) a

farm of more than fifty acres. Though last
year was prosperous, two hundred thousand
emigrated, a large proportion to the United
States, which held out every inducement. In
this way skilled artisans became expatriated
and also alienated. Surely, then, it is the duty
of Parliament to give attention to the subject.
Land should be offered at so low a price that
the bait would take, and the emigrants be
enabled at once to settle on their own lands.
The integrity of the Empire would be main-
tained, for we should thereby be planting loyal
men in all parts of it.
Such were the views which the member

support of Sir HARRY VERNEY, Mr. KINNAIRD,

indeed, qualifying his support with this
remark, that emigration is at present as large
as desirable, and that any scheme for pro-
moting it on a large scale would rouse opposi-
tion from employers, yet agreeing fully in the
desirability of directing emigration to our own
colonies rather than to the United States.
The UNDER SECRETARY for the Colonies
made the usual sort of reply, half concession,
half evasion. He approved generally of the
views expressed by the hon. gentleman. But
they opened up very wide questions; a great
deal was to be said for, but more against. A
deal would depend on whether it was intended
to supply colonial wants or to 'relieve Imperial

considerable. The money sent home by emi-

Australia and New Zealand, and the total sent
between 1848 and 1870 was no less than
£18,334,000. That showed great providence,
but if the State interfered, they would stop that
healthy and unaided emigration. Then a
healthy internal emigration was going on in
the country itself, which it would not be wise
to interfere with. Thus the official conclusion
is, that much might- be done, but nothing
needs to be done, and nothing is to be done.
This, however, was said in so thin a House,
that the subject . will be raised again, when
Mr. MA.orrE gets his returns.

REVIEWS.

re Ballot ; and Corruption and Expenditure
at Election's, A Collection of Essays and
Addresses of different Dates. By W. D.
Christie, M.A., C. 8., formerly Her Majesty's
Minister to the Argentine Confederation,
and to Brazil; Author of the "Life of the
First 2arl of Shaftesbury." London:
Macmillan and Co., 1872.
Some months ago we reviewed in these
Columns a work of some historical interest by
Christie. The work above mentioned has
a special interest-in connection with the con-
tests of the present generation. On the
former occasion we referred to the author's
earnest efforts and sacrifices on behalf of the
popular cause at a time when the people had
not se many defenders, nor were so well able
Lo support them as now. Apart, therefore,
from the value of the contents of this little
volume as a particularly seasonable contribu-
tion to the right side in a great struggle for
freedom and purity of election, we are glad to
be able to refer our readers to the evidence
contained in it of the statements we formerly
made as to Mr. Christie's services in his
earlier days.
But the fact is, that the arguments and facts
brought forward in the essays and speeches
now published, are an overflowing magazine
of arms and ammunition for the struggle that
has been going on for about forty years
against corruption and intimidation at elec-
tions; against the disgraceful and cancerous
wickedness whereby the liberties of the people,
and political progress generally, have been
stunted and poisoned at their very roots. As
We read the exhaustive arguments of the prin-
cipal essay. in Mr. Christie's volume, "An
Argument in favour of the Ballot" (originally
published as a pamphlet in 1839), or the bril-
liant .speech the delivered in the House of
Commons, June 21, 1842, or his strenuous
pleadings for measures against electoral
corruption, with suitable remedies, in 1864,
1866, and 1869, we do not wonder at men
like John Stuart Mill and the Rev. F. D.
Maurice, speaking highly of our author's en-
deavours.
To the pamphlet on "Election Ccituption
and its Remedies," Mr. Mill alluded thus in
the Houseof Commons, March 26, 1868 :
"I will make n suggestion, which will be found
in a pamphlet which has attracted a good deal of
attention, and has been read, I know, by members
of the Government. It is written by Mr. W. D.
Christie, formerly a member of this House, and
who, I hope, may be so again."

Mr. Mill also said, in reference to the " sug-
gestions " for restraining corrupt expendi-
ture

"Great crodit is due to Mr. Christi° for having,
as it seems to me, hit the right nail on the
head."

The following- is even more emphatic testi-
mony. Mr. Mill, writing to Mr. Christie in
1868, says :
"you have thought to greater purpose on the
means of preventing electoral corruption, and are
likely to be of more serivibein passing measures for
that highly important fida; than any other person
that I could name."

The Rev. F. D. Maurice, commenting OIL the
"suggestion' &c., in an article to be found
in A' Macmillan's Magazine," July, 1864,
gives the weight of his high character and
ability to the flame view

" Nothing map do more to justify. the existence
Of this Association (The Social Science Associa-
tion), than an effortto which Mr. Christie, the late
minister inl3razil, has incited it in an admirable
killper, in which he has proposed an organisation
or the restraint of corruption and expenditure at
elections "

, gladly endorse these opinions, though
any testimony of oars is little needed after
that of men so eminent; but we invite our
readers to examine the book and judge for
tileinsolvaa. We ghoul(' bathe less anxious to
Press the subject on their notice, were it not
that we are only too well aware to what an
Mont all the corrupt expenditure, no less
than We direct bribery and intimidation, were
praoticed at elections, tends not only to
demoralise the 'working classes in small
boroughs, but to keep up an iniquitous pro-
Party qualifieation for members of the House
of Coramone, and to keep out of that 1101180
!lien in all respects qualified to represent the
Mdustrial (dams. Those disgraceful proceed-
ings are largely, the cause of the people's
House of Parliament being filled with wealthy
men, and the representatives of capital, of the
army, and of the legal profession, while not
single working man has yet been able to
obtain a Oat diero. -
The following_ account of the political
situation Trku.,#r. ,Christie made his rather
memorable. speech in that House, Jane ,21,
1842, will be ;pad with some interest at the
Present time.
"I was a member of the House of Commons,
Bitting for Weymouth, when Mr. 1.1. G. Ward,
member for ghefilsid, Who WAS afterwards Sir
Henry Ward find died Governor of Madras,
brought forward the question of the Ballot, on
June 21, 1842. The Conservative Were then in
Power, and Sir Robert Peel Prime Minister.
Grote had retired from Parliament on the dissolu-
tion of the previous year. There was an amicable
rivalry between Mr. 'Ward and Mx, Sheif, as to who

should take up the queation ; the latter gave way.
Mr. Ward's motion was seconded by Mr. Henry
Berkeley. Silence reigned on the Gld'vernment
side; no one rose to reply from the Conservative
benches. A third speech was made in favour of
the Ballot by a Liberal member, Captain Layard.
Again, when he sat down, no one rose. I then
delivered the following speech, which had the
effect of bringing up a highly respected Conserva-
tive member, Mr. Granville Vernon, who said that
he was especially tempted to rise to protest
against the remonstrance addreased by the member
for Weymouth, in forcible language to the First
Lord of the Treasury.' The debate thus begun
went on. The speakers for the Ballot were Cap-
tain Berkeley (afterwards Lord Fitzhardinge),
Captain Bernal (now Mr. Bernal Osborne), Mr.
Charles Ponsonby (now Lord Do Manley), Mr.
Morgan John O'Connell, Mr. Shiel, Mr. Serjoant
Murphy, Mr. O'Connell (the groat O'Connell);
and Mr. Wakley; the speakers against were Mr.
Monckton Milnes (now Loki Houghton), Mr.
Byng, Lord John Manners Sir Tames Graham,
and Lord John Russell. On the division, there
were 167 for, and 290 against, the Ballot. The
numbers in 1839, when Mr. Grote last proposed
the measure, were 217 for and 335 against.
"When I sat down on that occasion, Mr. O'Con-
nell, who Was sitting under me, asked my excel-
lent colleague and friend, Mr. Bernal, who was so
long Chairman of Committees, to introduce me to
him, and I had thus the honour of making that
celebrated man's acquaintance. The subject of
corruption at elections was prominent in the
course of 1842, owing to the number of election
petitions which followed the general election of
1841, and to a number of compromises to avoid
discovery, which led, at Mr. Roebuck's instance,
to the appointment of a special Committee of
Inquiry. r
Mr. Christie concluded thus :

"I believe, candidly, that the Ballot will not
do mischief in any proportion to its good, and
that it will effectually diminish the evils of intimi-
dation and bribery, which now so widely prevail,
and the effects of which are to degrade voters,
lower the tone of feeling among persons who resort
to those practices, and foil the purpose for which
the Reform Bill has bestowed the franchise. And if
the Ballot will do this, it cannot now surely be need-
ful, when every day unfolds to us some new tale
of corrupt* worse than that which went before,
to impress on the House the necessity of adopting
it. Rather would I say that, next to giving bread
to those Who are starving, it is our first duty to
stay this &oral pestilence which is spreading, and
whitib; as it spreads, destroys honour' virtue,
truth, courage, manliness, among the humbler
orders of Our society. When I have heard the
right honourable baronet (Sir It. Peel), who is at
the head of the Government, more than once
make his new tariff and his income tax the reason
for postponing investigations into bribery, and
declining to undertake legislation on the subjeot,
I have thought that this`was not the course which
should be taken by the First Minister of the
country on a question more vitally than any other
affecting the morals of the nation, and, as a moral
question requiring his first care. Talk of the
credit of the country, and its military renown, and
the glory of our commerce and manufactures,
which Income tax and tariff are to foster and
enhance: why, when the virtue ancl morality of
the people are in peril, and aspirants to the legis-
lature and to power are doing their worst to make
slaves and hirelings of electors, and perverting
institutions given, for freedom'b sake, and to ele-
vate the holders of the franchise, to the enslaving
and debasing of qur countrymen, is it not time to
reflect that, when the internal element of greatness
have gone, material,prosperity and fame among the
nations are only so much gilding and tinsel hiding
filth and rottenness within P If you will adopt the
motion of the honourable member for Sheffield,
you will serve the cause of morality, and while
vindicating our .electoral institutions and . pre-
paring for their further development, will give a
worthy impulse to the social and political progress
of the nation.

We earnestly hope that the faithful advo-
cates of this important measure may sea it
triumphantly carried during the present Ses-
sion, and that they may also see other efficient
moans taken for preventing electoral corrup-
tion. Would that one of the earliest, and for
a time ahnost solitary, advocates of the Ballot,
Mr. Orote, could have witnessed that triumph.
Still more we regret that it is not to be twoom.
pulled during ihis Session by a measure not
inferior to the Bailot in importance, viz., for
throwing the expenses of elections on the rates.
The monopoly of Parliamentary power by
wealth is still too strong for justioo.

THE 'WORKING OF THE EDUCATION
ACT.

The following report was made by the Vice
President in the House on Thursday.
Mr. Dixon asked the Vice President of the
Council whether he would inform the House
of the number of boroughs and parishes in
England and Wales respectively in which
school boards have been formed, and of the
number of school districts in which there exists
a deficiency of educational provisions, exclusive
of those where school boards have been formed,
and in how many of these deficient districts the
department has taken steps to cause the forma-
tion of school boards.
Mr. W. E. Forster: In reply to my hon,
friend's first question, I may state that school
boards have -been formed in 88 boroughs in
England and in 11 boroughs in Wales ; and, as
regards parishes not boroughs, in 120 in En,,0.-
land and 125 in Wales. The House may like
to be informed what proportion these numbers
bear to the total number of boroughs and
parishes. There are 224 municipal boroughs
and about 14,800 parishes not boroughs in the
kingdom; so that, taking together England
and Wales, there are 92 out of 224 boroughs
and 245 out of 14,800 parishes in which
the compulsory formation of school boards
bag been anticipated by lobe' action.
These figure's would, however, by themselves
give a very unfair impression and merely
Mislead the House and the public.
If, instead of the numbers of boroughs and
parishes, we take the population, I find that
the population of these ninety-nine boroughs
in which there are school boards is about
5,200,000, while the population of the 125
boroughs in which there are no school boards
is only about 1,200,000. (Hear, hear.) Again,
while the total population of the 18,000
parishes net boroughs is about 13,000,000,
the population of the 245 in which there
are school boards is more than 1,100,000.
The average population of these 245 parishes
is about 4,550,000, while the average of the
large number of others is only 820. The fact
is, the larger the school district the larger
in all probability the school deficiency, and
therefore the greater the difficulty of its pro-
vision without the assistance of the rates,
The inhabitants of a large borough or of a
populous manufacturing
...village, seeing that a
rate is inevitable, ask for it at once, while in
a small rural parish there is a hope and an
effort to avoid a rate by voluntary subscrip-
d i
on. But in either case there s a most
praiseworthy desire to make the needful pro-
vision to meet the educational wants of the
I,district without waiting for the central office
to compel such provision, and I feel sure that
, the House will gratefully acknowledge the
general, and .1 may say the wonderful, re-
sponse which has been made throughout the
kingdom, not only in the towns, but
also in the rural parishes, by the measure
which we passed only a year and a half ae,,,0.
(Hear, hear.) Adding the metropolis, which,
as the House, is aware, is under a school board
by the Act, the total population in England
and Wales already under sohool boards is
9,640,887, or about three-sevenths of the
population of England, and about one-third
of the population of Wales. This differenee
between England and Wales is, not because
school boards are less popular in Wales the
contrary is the fact; but because in W*ales
the agricultural families bear. a large propor-
tion to the towns. I must take this oppor-
tunity to state another fact which wilt interest
all those members who are watching_ the
experiment of Compulsory attendance. When
I had charge of the Education Bill I Ventured
to prophesy that such compulsion would be
tried in some largo towns, and that the
opinion of the country in its favour would
be found to be stronger than was generally
supposed. My ezpeotation has been inert)
than *firmed by the experience of the last
few months. The school boards of London,
Liverpool, Manchester, Bristol, and of almost
all the large towns, and of several of the
smaller districts, have bravely grappled with
this difficulty, and bye-laws for compul-
sory attendance have been already passed
by 118 school boards, having within their
districts a population of about 8,000,000,
more than one third of the population of the
kingdom. (Hear, hear.) I come now to my
hon. 'friend's second question.. He asks me
in how many school districts, where
there are no school boards, there is
educational deficiency. To this question
I can give him no definite answer
to-day, although I hope to .be able to
i
do so n a few weeks. The reason is, that the
educational survey of the country is not yet
quite completed, and I think hon. members will
not be Surprised at this statement when they
remember that this survey has to be made
over more than 16,000 districts, and that our
°fibers have not only to *ascertain the number
of wheels and children, but whether these
ischools are or are not efficient and suitable,
and a most difficult question whether
parishes should or should not be grouped
together. Our reports are, however, now
quickly corning in, and, though the dept.irt-
meat is hard worked in meeting the regime-
Meats of that half of the kingdom which is
already under school beards, we shall, I hope,

I very soon begin to compel the supply of that
' school accommodation which may be proved
to be deficient in the other half. As yet we
have issued no orders for 'school boards
except under section 12 of the Act; but
before the end of next month we expect to
begin to issue our notices of deficiency of
school accommodation under section 9.
(Cheers.)
Mr. Dixon asked the Vice-President of the
Council if he could state the number of de-
nominational schools to which grants had been
made since the Ist of August, 1870, and the
amount of said grants; the number of appli-
cations for building grants still under consider.
ation and the estimated amount of grants
still to be made, and the number of suoh ap-
plications which have been declined...
Mr. W. E. Forster: The number of schools
to which building grants have been made
since August 1, 1870, is 999, and the amount
of such grants is £168,131 ; of these 948 are
denominational schools, with an amount of
£160,850. When I say that these grants
have been made I do not moan that they have
been paid, but that the proposals of the mana-
gers have been accepted, and that payment is
promised on the buildings being completed.
There are still 1,001 applications in progress;
of these 1,287 have been approved by the
office, subject to the fulfilment of conditions
as regards plans and other details. There re-
main 614 which have not reached the stage of
approval or disapproval, chiefly because their
promoters have not given the necessary in-
formation. The number of applications which
have been refused is 243, and 191 have been
withdrawn. My hon. friend asks me the esti-
mated amount of grants still to be made. To
this question loan give him no precise answer,
as every one of the applications which is not
passed is subject to such deductions as may
result from inquiry by the Department.
As, however, the building grant bill is a
matter of much interest, I will endeavour to
make a guess at its amount. No money,
as I have stated, is actually paid until we
have a certifieate of the completion of the
building. It is possible that of the 999 schools
for which we have promised payment on com-
pletion Home will not be actually built. It iv
probable; that this will be the case with a still
laiger ploportion of the 1,287 which we have
appreved ;' and I expect to hear nothing more
of a large number of the remaining 614. Taking
into account all these probable deductions and,
estimates, the grants still to promise at £l6B
each, the average of the 999 already promised,
I think I shall make an outside guess if I ests.
mate the total building grants to be paid in
respect of applications since the passing of the
Act at about £400,000 to about 2,400 schools
and taking a rough average, providing school
accommodation for about 400,000 children.
This £400,000 may appear a large sum out of
the taxes, but it must be remembered that it
will he a much larger saving to the rates.
(Hear, hear.) We find, taking the average
of the last four years, that the Parliamentary
grant is slightly less than 1-sth of the total

if my estimate be,correot, finishup our building
grant system by a grant of £400,000, to which-
private individuals will have subscribed
£1,600,000, and we shall have provided schools
for 100,000 children, which without this grant
and this voluntary subscription would have 4
required an outlay of £2,000,000 out of the
local rates. (Hear, hear.)
