THE BERMONDSEY WORKING
MEN'S CLUB. -

A meeting of the above club took place on
February 13th. Lord Claud Hamilton took the
chair, supported by H. B. Praed, Esq. (Presi-
dent), Samuel Sevington, Esq., Walter Dixon,
Esq., Mr. Thomas Patteson, and other gentle.
men.

The report was read by the Secretary (Mr.
House), which showed a surplus of £2O Os. 3d.,
after defraying all working expenses.
Samuel Bevington, Esq., moved the adop-
tion of the report and balance-sheet, in which
he said that it was the most successful club
he had heard of; inasmuch as it had fulfilled
its mission, and was a great benefit both to the
employers and the employed. He stated that
the employers were greatly indebted to the
President for having founded, such an institu-
tion, and he hoped that they would show they
appreciated his efforts by removing the
balance of the opening account. He also
gave .£5 for the firm he represented, and £2
as a private donation.
Walter C. Dixon, Esq., seconded its adop-
tion, in which he said that it was an institution
that helped working men to help themselves;
it was not true that working men would not
meet together except for boozing, when he
found that the profits realized from refresh-
ments amounted to £7B 14s. Od., and no
intoxicating drinks sold.
Mr. MAW (a moderate drinker) Moved—
" That in the opinion of this meeting, the
introduction of intoxicating drinks into work-
ing men's clubs is not necessary to make them
successful."

Seconded by Mr. House, in which he said elubs
with intoxicating drinks were 'only public-
houses without the restrictions of the law ;
even the better olass of them do not advocate
its introduction in all, but admit that the
Sunday morning drinking is a groat evil, be.
i cause members ntroduce their friends, and
thus evade the law. He also said that the
_kelt. IL Solly stated that working men
should have some privilege that the West-
end clubs enjoy, but in his suggestions to the
Home Secretary he out away every privilege
they enjoy, by closing them at the same time
as the public) house. Mr. Marsh (a moderate
drinker) supported it.
There being two meetings in the club (be-
cause the large room would not accommodate
all), the above resolutions were put to both
and carried unanimously.
Previous to these meetings, an open air
meeting was held in Bermondsey-square.
The club band attended, and resolutions to
the same effect were carried by about 3,000
persons.

During the meeting in the club, his lord.
ship sang a Bono., entitled, "A. rose leaked
in at the window" (composed by himself),
which was received with loud applause.
A vote of thanks to the chairman • and
president terminated the proceedings. "

THE SA.T.,FORD SCHOOL-RATE CASE.-
'SALE OF M.R. WARBURTON'S FUR-
NITURE. •

The sale by public auction Of the furniture
which, undera warrant of distress, had been
taken from the house of Mr. William War-
burton, a member of the Salford School Board,
on the ground of his refusal to pay the school
rate on his property in Salford, took place
on Tuesday afternoon in the police parade
room, at the Salford Town Hall. The articles
seized were a a circular rosewood 100 'table,
supported by a solid carved pillar, with claws,
and a rosewood drawing-room chair. The
amount of the 'school rate which had been
assessed upon Mr. Warburton was 18s. 9d. ;
but the total charges incurred in connection
with the legal proceedings in the ease in-
creased it to aboat R 2 10s. Mr. James
Appleyard, No. 34, Prazenose-street, was the
auctioneer who conducted the sale. . The
attendance was not numerous, and the whole
transaction, commencing at two p.m.t was
concluded in a few minutes. The auctioneer
said he would first offer the table to pur-
chasers, and requested a bid for it. After a
short pause .£2 7s. was named as a price, and
then £2 10s. Thirteen more bids followed,
each of them, with a single exception, being
ss. in advance of the preceding One ; • and the
table was finally sold to Mr. Charles Thomas
Chievers, of Shaw Heath, Stockport. The
proceedings had hitherto been conducted
quietly, but a portion of the company now
began to sing, For he's a jolly good fellow,"
and one voice called out, "That's for the sup-
port of a greedy church presided over by a
aucceaser from Peterloo." The auctioneer I
Said he should not sell the remaining lot, as
the sum already obtained was sufficient to
cover the amount demanded from Mr. War-
burton. The gentleman who purchased the
table acted on behalf of a number of persons
who purpose restoring it to Mr. Warburton.

articles.text:
THE NEW EDUCATION CODE. •

The new code of regulations for the present
year, as drawn up by the Committee of the
Privy Council on Education, has been pub-
lished. Several modifications, as compared with
last year's code, appear in the new regulations.
Among them it is provided that tha managers
of a school which has met not less than
80 times in the evening in the course of a year
may claim for every scholar who has attended
not less than 50 evening meetings of the
school 7s. 6d., subject to examination—viz.,
2s. 6d. for passing in reading, 2s. 6d. for
passing in writing, and 28. 6d. for passing
in arithmetic. The grant is reduced as fol-
lows : (a) By its excess above the income of
the school from fees, rates, and subscriptions;
the rate of 15s. per scholar, according to the
average number in attendance; and one half
the expenditure on the annual maintenance
of the school in the year defined by article
13, (b) By not less than one-tenth nor
more than one-half in the whole, upon the
inspector's report, for faults of instruction or
discipline on the part of the teacher, or
(after six months' notice) for failure on the
part of the managers to remedy any such
defect in the premises as seriously interferes
with the efficiency of the school, or to pro-
vide proper furniture, books, maps, and
other apparatus of elementary instruction. If
the inspector at a visit of surprise not less
than six mouths after notice has been given
of the requirements of the Education depart-
ment reports that they have not been carried
into effect, a deduction may be made from the
next grant to the school. (e) At the rate of
£2O for the year, for every 40 scholars, after
the first 20, of the average number in at-
tendance, unless there has been during
the year one pupil teacher fulfilling
the conditions of article 70, for every
such 40 scholars. A certificated assistant
teacher, or an assistant fulfilling the con-
ditions of article 79, is equivalent to two
pupil teachers. (d) By is. per scholar, ac-
cording to the average number in attendance
throughout the year, unless vocal music
forms a part of the ordinary course of instruc-
tion.

articles.text:
WORKMEN'S HALL, SOUTHAMPTON.

The half-yearly general meeting for the
Purpose of receiving the auditors' report on
the balance sheet and for the electing a com-
mittee of management and officers for the
ensuing six months took place on Tuesday
evening. The balance sheet showed a balance
of £l4 Bs. 3d. and was unanimously adopted.
The Goal club account showed that 420 tons
11 owts. of coal had been supplied to 750
members during the past six 'months. The
savings' bank account showed that £22 88. 4d.
had been deposited during the half-year by
its -members. A oommittee of management
was duly elected with Mr. W. B. George as
chairman, Mr. Walter Jaokman, re-elected
treasurer, Messrs. Tanner and Dewey auditors,
Messrs, George Brazin, Mo'Leod, and Sharpe
truptees, and Mr. George Gordon re-elected
secretary. The following donations were
stated to have been received during the past
six months; Mr. Burgess, Ms.; Messrs. Baker
and 10s. ' • Mr. Thornbaok, 2s. 6d.; Mr.
Lewis Co.,owell, 2s. 6d.; and Mrs. Rayner, the
'Southampton Observer. The Chairman, in his
remarks, hoped the time was not far distant
hen,they would have the pleasure of meeting
In a more suitable building than the one they
had to meet in now, and he sincerely hoped
that some of our leading townsmen would
kindly come forward. and assist the committee
in their endeavours to get a new hall worthy
of the, town, so that the working men could
have a suitable place for reading and dis-
cussion, for it would be, the means of inducing
many working men to give the hall the
Preference over the public-houses, should the
committee meet with the success which they
all desire to obtain. The chairman then
suggested that there should be a building
committee for that purpose, and Messrs.
Brazier, Wills, Powell, and Dewey, were duly
elected the building committee. A vote of
thanks to the ,retiring ofifoers and chairman
brought the meeting to a close.

On Wednesday, the council of the Evan-
gelical Alliance, at the Alliance House, Adam.
Street, Strand, passed the following re-
solution :--" That, considering the mis-
understanding which has arisen with regard
to the interpretation of the treaty between
England and the United States of America,
the council of the Evangelical Alliance invite
their members and Christians generally, at
this conjuncture, to unite in public and
Private prayer to Almighty God that the rulers
of both countries may be graciously influenced,
and led to adopt those measures which make
for the continuance of peace and goodwill bet-
ween the nations." The council trust that this
invitation will be generally embraced and
responded to.—. Rock.

Were last week charged at the Marylebone

gay committed for trial.

IMPROVIDENCE _OF THE WORKING

To the Editor of the BEE HIVE.

_
SIR,—I do not know whether I. shall be

The part I allude to is his criticism of the
speech of Sir C. Trevelyan which I cannot
look upon, and I am sure many will agree with
me, as being so absurd as Mr. Howell appears
to consider it, for if Mr. Howell is as well
acquainted with the habits of the working
classes, as I suppose him to be, he must know
that it is an undeniable fact that unfortunately

("sometimes by those who can least afford it") at

A WORKING M.

POLITICAL PARTIES.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

St:a,—lt can hardly be questioned that the
signs of the times point to a not far distant
disruption of existing parties. The recent
political agitations bound together for a time
certain antagonistic elements which are now, in
the face of social differences, resolving them-
selves into a normal state. The shibboleth of
parties is changing_. That which was their
rallying ery yesterday is forgotten in that of
to-day. The onward strides of democracy has
so far weakened the ties of party by its on-
slaught on the feudal system of governmentby
a few of the "great families "of the land, that
a thoughtful politician now-a-days is some-
thing more than a mere blind follower of a
party leader. It is not sufficient for a man,
because he was a Liberal last year and voted
for certain much-needed. reforms that be is to
do the same this year, in spite of conscientious
objections to the contrary, and then defend
himself on the ground of party allegiance.
There has been no greater hindrance to the
passing of certain social reforms than our
system of party and party government. No
matter how great the need or how excellent the
remedy, if the measure was introduced by one
party, that fact was sufficient to ensure the
opposition of the other, _

After the disposal of the Ballot Bill, social
questions will undoubtedly be paramount.
But in the discussions of these questions, the
same faith which secured a eonourrenee of
thought and unity of aotion in the past, may
not now suffice. A man may have been a firm
supporter of household or manhood suf-
frage, with the Ballot, and the other subjects
that formed the Liberal creed, and yet be unable
conscientiously to support the disestablishment
of the English Church or the establishment of
a purely secular system of Education. His
faith may not incline him to accept those
extreme measures with regard to the liquor
traffic, which so delight our teetotal friends;
and yet he may as earnestly desire the refor-
mation of the drunkard as they do. Calling
a man a Liberal or a Conservative does not
invest him with a monopoly of wisdom. HA
may be a "bright particular star" in the fir-
mament of his party, and still be thought a
great fool by worldly outsiders.
After the many times the interests of
working men have been sacrificed to the
interests of party, it is wonderful the power
which can still be exerted by the sound of the
party drum. After the unprotected condition
in which the miners were left for years
by the continuesi postponement of the
Mines Regulation Bill, • and the trick
played upon the trades' unionists ge-
nerally, by the adoption by the Commons
of the Lords' Amendments to the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, nothing short
of an entire separation from either party
ought to have sufficed. In the coming
political turmoil let us act as a party to our-
selves, and snatch from the hands of the
great combatants, the rights they deny .0
when all is peace. In the United States, the
men of labour have gathered together a party
or union which has its influence upon publio
affairs. Why cannot we do the same? Why?
—Because of the ,jealousy of the working men
themselves ; of the ill-natured feelings with
which Many regard those who have the
misfortune to act as leaders in the industrial
army, and because of the shortsightedness
which induces a large number to ignore their
own special questions in favour of their
" party, ' whatever that may be. In return
for this support, what has the party done for
us as workmen? Have they done anything
special for us, without our having to watch
and pray in earnest for it. Is the Trade Union
Act anti its companion, The Criminal Law
Amendment Act, such: an unmixed good that
we can afford to be thankful for the boon ? It
is because of this that I say let us iota the

coming orisis,• for out of it may come some
good to us, if we are watchful. A,lthough a
Radical, I hold that the Liberal party has not
done justice to us as workmen in the past,
and that we are fully justified in standing on
our defence.—l am, &0.,, _ _

CHARLES' STEVENS.

SOLUTION OF THE DIFFICULY
BETWEEN LABOUR. AND CAPITAL.
To the Editor of the BEE-HITS.
Sir,--Recently a good deal has been said
about the relations between labour and
capital. No satisfactory settlement of the
queston, however, can take place unless cei-
tain sine qua none are duly attended to.
With regard to the men these are. 1, a legal
status. 2, a career. 3. elasticity in the
wages. 4, inexhausted energies. 5, contin-
ual work. 6, protection against competition—
especially that by the masters. While the
masters require guarantees for-1, civility in
the workman. 2, efficiency in the same. 3,
fulfilment of contracts. 4, sufficiency of
work. .5, repayment of advances. 6, general
good behaviour and honesty.
These conditons, severally and jointly
can be best secured by the following plan—viz.,
1, divide the trades into guilds, and enact that
no workman follow his craft unless he be amem-
ber of a guild; also (a) that the guilds be go-
verned by a president, vice-presidents, and
committee with the assistance of a treasurer
and secretary selected from the members. (b)
that all the officers be appointed wholly by the
guilds excepting the president, whose appoint-
ment be confirmed by the Government.
(o) that the president lodge substantial
security" with the Government for the supply
at all times, on demand, of a full complement
of efficient men, and for the proper working of
the guild. This will give dignity and status
to the trades; and guard the masters against
any misbehaviour and disrespect on the part
of the men.

2. Divide the workmen further into
classes with wages corresponding to the divi-
sions, for instance (a) apprentices, on intro-
ductory wages; (b) ordinary workmen on
subsistence allowance; o) first-class hands, on
remunerative wages; d) superior workmen,
on full remuneration; e) foremen on salaries.
With the understanding that promotion from
one grade to the other be by competition, and
raade by the guilds in full council assembled;
and that OA every job a certain number of the
inferior workmen the apprentices excepted,
carry one of the higher grades who is to be
generally responsible for the work. This will
insure the necessary career to the workmen,
and at the same time afford ample guarantee
as to their efficiency.
3.—Regulate the wages according to the
rise and fall of provisions, taking the food,
staples, rent, and the price of clothing as the
bases lof calculation, and ordain (a) that a
price list of wages be drawn up monthly, in
advance, for every trade for the guild com-
mittee and the police. (b) , That the list be
certified to by the chief commissioner of
police, and hung up at the police courts and

To the Editor of the BEli-HivE;
SIR,—My attention has been called to a
singular letter from Professor Beesly, inserted
in the Times of the oth inst. He says :
" For once we are
"Some of us who have the misfortune to be in
a state of habitual antagonism to the opinions
of our countrymen are now experiencing the
pleasurenf being in harmony with every one
we meet on the most important of immediate
questions." This humble and submissive
utterance is quickly followed by a bit of tall
talk and bad-tempered advice, in these words
—" If our offer is rejected, as seems likely to
be the ease, justice does not oblige us' and
dignity forbids us, to renew it. I trust that,
at whatever cost, the present and all future
governments would steadily refuse to enter
into any negooiations growing out of the
American war. I contemplate a war with as
much horror as anyone; but if it is thrust
upon us, we must accept it, and of this the
Americans may be assured, that this nation
will never have appealed to arms with such
reluctance, yet with such entire unanimity."
To me, sir, this sort of language to a
friendly people like the Americans, at a
moment when a grave misunderstanding has
arisen between our bungling diplomats and
their 'cute lawyers, is as unbecoming, as un-
worthy of England's "dignity," and as un-
likely to lead to any good on either side as
were the acrid appeals to English working
men of this same Professor a few months ago,
when Paris was in flames. It is an old saying
that "Positive people are generally
.in the
wrong." Auguste Comte is not happy in his
exponents of to-day; they seem irritable un-
practical folk, difficult to get on with in
minor matters, and most surely not be trusted
to speak to the helmsman when our political
barometer falls towards "stormy."—Yours,
PAX.
London, Feb. 10.

P.S.—I should not have troubled you with
this, but that Professor Beesly's name is so
well known among republicans, democrats,
and demagogues on both sides of the Atlantic,
that his letter might lead the Americans to
infer that we had all caught the Professor's
complaint, which is hardly yet the ease.
Sensible men still contemplate an early and
"an amicable settlement.'
